utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. May I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence. That still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, and thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, would you be so kind as to explain the difference between an observation post, a command post, and a headquarters staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These three concepts are closely interrelated to the concept of command in the army. Observation posts are organised by squad leaders, platoon leaders, and company leaders or commanders. A command post is organised by a battalion command, a brigade command and higher levels of command. Headquarters staff is a professional body or organ which for the needs of higher levels of command, professionally analyses problems and suggests how the unit should be used in keeping with the assignment that was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear of Stanko Vujanovic's house where Captain Radic's observation post was as being used at any point as a command post or as headquarters for liberating Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of that having been a command post. The command post of the 1st Battalion was in the street of Svetozara Markovica which I stated to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since during the course of this trial, for a while we had some dilemmas in this courtroom, what is a komandir and what is a komandant? As someone who took immediate part in command and was subordinated to a company commander, can you definitely explain from a military professional point of view, what is a commander in the sense of a komandir and what is a commander in the sense of komandant?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Komandir is the lowest level of command in terms of a person, an individual. In our army, komandirs are squad leaders, platoon leaders and company leaders. Further on, commanders in the sense of komandant are battalion commanders, brigade commanders, division commanders, corps commanders and so on. That is to say that the concept of komandir is one that pertains to a lower level of command, because up to the level of company commander there are no headquarters. There is no staff as a professional organ. There is not a body that works for the commander in order to assist him make his decisions. That is to say that a company commander does not have its own staff. Only an assistant commander, that is to say a person who helps him from the point of view of logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. While you were in Vukovar, did you hear of Vojislav Seselj, president of a political party at that time, visiting Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that the mentioned person did pay a visit to the theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this, anything?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that one morning during the regular preparation of tasks, the commander of the Leva Supoderica Detachment came to our command, Milan Lancuzanin. He said to me that during the course of the previous day, Mr. Vojislav Seselj had come to his unit. He asked me whether I had the time or ability to attend or, rather, why I did not attend this gathering. I said to Milan that our command post is in the street of Svetozara Markovica and that that is where we receive guests.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major Tesic, as commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion, did he go to the command post of group south and did that happen every day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the 1st Motorised Battalion and the temporary composition of the 1st Assault Detachment, Major Tesic, in his role of commander, sometimes he would go there several times a day. From time to time he would go every three or four days for briefings, but he was the only person who went to the Supreme Command, the only one from among us who went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stijakovic, you have already stated that after some 20 days or so, after the attack began, local -- the local detachment, the Leva Supoderica, was engaged as well and that the commander of this detachment was Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni. My question is, and I'm asking whether you agree with this, Lancuzanin, once he was attached to JOD 1, did he receive tasks from the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When, in accordance with the order issued on the 29th of October, the order issued by the superior command, the assault detachment was established, and I represented its composition on a sketch yesterday, the commander of the Leva Supoderica Detachment was Milan Lancuzanin. In this way, he, from that day onwards, came and received tasks from the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The commander of the Territorial Defence, Vukovar, was Captain First Class Dusan Jaksic, as you said. My question is: In a given period of time, was he replaced and who was it that replaced him; do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the commander of the Petrova Gora Detachment was Captain Jaksic and that person, in accordance with the mentioned order, from the 29th of October, regularly came to receive tasks and assignments and to discuss matters with Major Tesic with a view to the pending tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before he appeared at the command post, he doesn't deny it, Jaksic stated that before he received orders from the commander of operative group south, Mrksic, was that before?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the assault detachment was established, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You've already explained that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, after that; that is to say, in accordance with the order issued on the 29th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And he received orders from Major Tesic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that in combat actions, Captain Radic was always in the combat disposition of his units, if you can answer that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic, during combat action, to the best of my knowledge, was a disciplined officer. Whenever he had to leave his unit, he asked Major Tesic for his permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did he come every day to the command post of the 1st Motorised Battalion and was that for the most part when the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion would return from the command post of operative -- Operations Group South?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As for the 3rd Motorised Company, it was attended on behalf of -- every briefing was attended only by Captain Radic. He was there on behalf of his company. He was the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember, since you already spoke about this, whether, at the regular briefing on the 20th, on the evening of the 20th, can you state this, can you confirm this with certainty, was Miroslav Radic there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What can you say as the superior officer, about Captain Miroslav Radic, company commander, during the Vukovar events?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a long story.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to say just a few sentences. Captain Radic is an officer who, before the combat action in Vukovar, always had problems with the officers within his unit. The problems were due to the fact that he did not have a sufficient number of officers, or rather that he had poor quality officers within his unit. To our great joy, about a month before combat started, Lieutenant Radivoje Vostic was transferred to that company and his duty was commander of the 1st Platoon and at the same time he was Radic's deputy. Then Captain Radic, for the first time, had an excellent officer, because Lieutenant Vostic completed the military academy as one of the best students there. At the theatre of war, these two officers, he, Captain Radic, and Lieutenant Vostic, displayed a high degree of responsibility for their men, care for their soldiers, and I know that from the first day of war, when a tank in Nova Ulica was stranded where there was an abandoned truck, I know that Captain Radic removed his soldiers so that they would not get harmed and he made a personal effort to pull out the tank crew. I know that Lieutenant Vostic, as an excellent officer, always led his group ahead, that is to say that he was at the head of the group, and as such, during the first days of the conflict, I remember sometime in the beginning of October, was it the 5th, was it the 4th, Lieutenant Vostic got killed. The death of Lieutenant Vostic affected Captain Radic by giving him a high degree of motivation. In his wish to carry out tasks received, he worked with even greater responsibility. We, the command, that is to say Tesic and I, often warned Captain Radic that he should take care of himself as well, bearing in mind the death of Lieutenant Vostic. I remember once there was this piece of news that Captain Radic had been wounded. We were very worried. It turned out that he had indeed been hit but that the shell hit his pistol. Even then he did not vacillate. In a soldierly, disciplined manner, he continued carrying out the task he had received. He was brave, responsible and resolute, but above all else, disciplined. I claim that not a single officer subordinated to us did not obey to such a degree. That is why his unit carried out the tasks received in the most successful way. That is why his road taken was the longest, all the way up to Milovo Brdo. That is why he was the first one who was proposed for an award leave to go home and visit his family. If the tasks that we had were to be repeated, I would again propose Captain Radic to carry them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stijakovic, I must forgotten about this or maybe it's something you didn't say at the outset about your military background in terms of which schools you completed before you took up your important posts in the JNA. So first there was the military academy but then you mentioned something else, too, didn't you? But you haven't quite finished your story. Is there anything very important that needs adding?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really of any relevance in relation to this event. I had completed the military academy, the political sciences faculty, certain advanced courses in the army. I was a teacher of tactics and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about after the war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war, I finished a specialised course for command staff officers at the academy in Belgrade. This was a brigade commander level training. After that I also completed the All People's Defence school, which is the highest possible level of training in the JNA, or what is today the army of Serbia. At both these academies, I performed in an exceptional manner and my grade point average was one of the highest ever. I am now an associate lecturer for military strategy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stijakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this concludes my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Domazet, are there any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Mrksic's Defence has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I won't be long. Although you see I've placed the lectern in front of me, I just need it to shuffle my papers for a little. Do I have a couple of questions for the witness, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, good morning to you, sir. I'm Novak Lukic. Now that I've introduced myself, can you please tell the Court first when you first met me, just to avoid any confusion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was second-last evening, two days ago, in the corridor of my hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did we meet for and what was the reason for us meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was you who had asked to see me in order to ask me about certain things that you say would be discussed at trial. Our conversation took between 15 and 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll say one thing. I wanted more time to talk to you but I had to leave more time for Mr. Radic's defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I was tired from my trip after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. You had arrived that same evening, hadn't you? I'll ask you something about the fighting in Vukovar. During the OTP case, we heard a lot about the fighting itself but not so much during our cases. Can you please take the war log? You have it in that set of documents in front of you, and if we could please have the following displayed on our monitors. This is the war log of the Guards Brigade, 401, Exhibit 401. The English reference is L 0100499, page 4 of the war log. Before you start looking at the war log, Mr. Stijakovic --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just take a minute to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll give you the page number but first let me ask you a question, if that's all right. Do you remember any incident where your ambulance was attacked?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe that for us? Who was it attacked by and what exactly occurred?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was right at the very beginning of combat action. In our unit we had a Pinzgauer ambulance. It was visibly marked with a red cross. The vehicle was driven by a driver and normally there was a doctor accompanying him. This team was supposed to go wherever anyone had been wounded, and based on an oath that doctors normally take they were duty-bound to provide medical assistance to any such persons regardless of the -- these persons' affiliation, whether they were Croat or Serb. And along the axis of the Motorised Company, where Captain Bojkovski was in charge, the 1st Motorised Company, the enemy at one point suddenly opened mortar fire, leaving two or three soldiers from his unit wounded. We quickly dispatched the ambulance, and since the street was an open area, while approaching the location of the wounded, the vehicle came under fire, under sniper fire to be more specific. When we got there, when they got there to help the wounded, again there was mortar fire. They came under mortar fire. As a result, the vehicle was hit but still moving. The doctor picked up the three wounded men, he took care of them, and once he was back he came to our command post to report what had happened, this being the reason I remember this with particular clarity. I also remember the doctor; he was shaking like a leaf.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the entry in the war log for the 2nd of October, 1600 hours? I thought it might be a good idea to have the English on the ELMO for the benefit of the Bench and that's why the reference I provided is the English reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll read it out loud and you just tell me if my reading is all right. "The village of Negoslavci, the 2nd of October, 1600 hours, commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion informs that an ambulance was hit and destroyed. Some were wounded." Is this in reference to the event you've just described?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Except the vehicle was not destroyed but there were wounded, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Another question in relation to the war log, the entry, generally speaking. In the fighting where your units were involved, what exactly was the fire-power of the enemy? Which sort of equipment were they using while fighting you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From day one of the fighting in Vukovar, I was truly surprised at the extent of good organisation, equipment, and personnel that the enemy deployed. All the artillery, the 120-millimetre mortars, the 60-millimetre mortars, anti-armour equipment and weapons and so on and so forth, mines, snipers, armour-piercing bullets and all that. I was really astonished at the sort of equipment that they had and that they were using. Secondly, I really marvelled at the organised manner and high professionalism which they used to organise the town's defence. In every location they seemed to have highly mobile intervention teams. And what's more important - and this is something that Mr. Jagetic explained to me on the very first day - the enemy had managed to get that section of town blocked off in its entirety. Not even a little bird could leave. Nobody could leave except by those roads that were under their control. To my knowledge, the only roads remaining under their control were the Bogdanovac road and a village road across the village of Luzac. My surprise was confirmed by the fact that when we finally freed the barracks we had to stay there for nearly 20 days. And it wasn't possible to move about for our manpower during the day precisely on account of the mortar and artillery fire, because when shells start falling, you know, people tend to run, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know it's a crystal clear answer from you, sir. I think we can now look at the list which I found in relation to the 9th of October at 1106 hours. I'm asking you, because this is in reference to your unit. I'll read it out loud for your benefit, sir. "At 1105, the commander" -- I'll just wait for you to find that reference.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same log?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The same log.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The 9th of October, 1100 hours. For the benefit of the Chamber in e-court this is L 0100514, page 19, but I believe we'll have it shortly.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1106. Is that the one you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It reads: "At 1105 the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment, Major Tesic, informs that along the front end he was under heavy fire from mortar Zoljas and hand-held rocket launchers." When they say "MB" I suppose that's mortars, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking for a comment from you because you've already said that all these weapons were being used by the enemy while fighting you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to another subject. We will be leaving this behind for the time being but now I'll ask you something in relation to my client. Thank you. We've heard evidence before this Court - and I think we are about to hear more, aren't we? - my client was often visiting, so to speak, the front line, wasn't he? What do you know about that? Did Sljivancanin ever come to tour your unit in your sector, so to speak, and how frequently in relation to other officers from the brigade, from the brigade command, and what were these visits like? It's my fault entirely, Mr. Stijakovic. Can you please pause after each of my questions and I'll try to pause after each of your answers in order to allow the interpreters sufficient time to do their job.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all right. Based on what I remember about the general mood and atmosphere at the battalion command, there were three persons who were particularly welcome when they came to visit our unit. The first being Colonel Mile Mrksic, the commander. The second being Major Veselin Sljivancanin. And the third such person being Major Stojkovic, the chief of engineers. This third person was unfortunately killed. At the command post of our unit the commander came less frequently. He always had accurate reports and he was absolutely up to date on what was going on in our unit. Major Sljivancanin was the one who came most frequently of all the command staff to the command post of the 1st Battalion. It's difficult for me to be very specific in terms of how many times he came but I'm certain that he came at least once a day. He would either phone or come over and see us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, sir, can you tell me what the reasons were for him coming and what I want to know most of all, as everybody else in this courtroom, did he ever issue any orders to you? To you, I mean your unit. I mean the command and I mean officers working in individual units, including those who you were coordinating and fighting with?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question. Major Sljivancanin held the post of chief of security in our unit. Given the fact that the 1st Motorised Battalion was physically the closest to the enemy, our command post was a mere 150 metres away from the Kruno Mesar building where paramilitary groups were stationed. It is only to be expected that as one goes about gathering intelligence on the enemy, whoever is doing that must approach the enemy as closely as possible, where the forces are in direct contact with the enemy, the 1st Motorised Battalion carried out its task on the 10th of November, which clearly tells you that this was a successful unit. It is only to be expected that this person would put in an appearance for the success to grow even greater, but also in order to establish contact with the population in the liberated area, as far as Milovo Brdo. As for the third reason, in our unit, the 1st Assault Detachment, we also had the TO detachment of Petrova Gora and that of Leva Supoderica. It is only to be expected that while coordinating business, all sorts of different business in the area, this person should be in control of the situation and should know exactly what is going on. Never, never and never did Major Sljivancanin order anything to Major Tesic. Never ever. Nor did he ever even try. Sometimes we would share a joke, perhaps. There was a bit of an atmosphere, you know. He was a merry person. And despite the fact that one of his sergeants had been killed over the previous days, his courier Zoran, he managed to overcome this due to his lightness of spirit. And that is why I suppose he came to see us so often, because that was the sort of atmosphere he found whenever he came. We were a group of people going about our business in a strictly professional manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You say he never gave any orders to Tesic, did he? Did you ever hear him give any orders to any other officer? And let me ask you straight away: Did he interfere with your work? When I say "your work," I mean your professional duties at any point in time whenever he came, whenever he talked to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember just before the close of combat action, we talked, and Mr. Sljivancanin paid me a compliment, given the fact that I was still a captain at the time in terms of rank and he was a major. He said, "Slavko, how come I didn't know you earlier? How come I didn't know you were this tough?" So this answers your question, I hope. There was absolutely no need for him to interfere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that's a sufficient answer and a very accurate one. Thank you. I would like to broach yet another topic with you. We've heard testimony here about the replacement of Dusan Jaksic and the appointment to his post of Miroljub Vujovic. We heard testimony that allegedly Sljivancanin had replaced Dusan Jaksic. My question to you first is whether you know whether there were any problems in terms of command and control performed by Jaksic? Did you know about it and what was actually done about it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for Mr. Jaksic's personality, he was a captain of the reserves, he was the commander of the Petrova Gora Detachment. I remember him as a lounge officer. He would always be clean shaven, his boots would be shiny. He was always spick and span, and as the fighting continued, I assume that he encountered ever more problems in his unit. I mean he personally. Because I never recall any of his reports in which it would be stated that he had led his group into attack or to carry out any tasks. And as days went by, and as combat actions developed, new people came to his unit. They were brave and they gained their authority in the field. For this reason, Jaksic lost his nerve and he simply did not dare issue any commands to his soldiers, and from time to time, he would get in conflicts with his subordinates but also with the Leva Supoderica Detachment, because the commander of that detachment was from the same area as he was. At one point, we had to get involved in their conflict. We had to try and achieve reconciliation and to get them to focus on their real task and not to squabble about the billeting, the logistics and so on. Up until the 29th of October, Captain Jaksic performed the tasks he received from his superior command. He was acting in concert with us. Once the assault detachment was established, he was under the command of Major Tesic. But it has never been our practice when a unit is attached to another unit, Major Tesic, this is our practice, would never replace a person or change anything in terms of the personnel of that unit. Why? Because that would result in yet another kind of problems for him, because then he would have to appoint somebody, his own man, and then he would be in a situation when he would be solving other people's problems. That is why we took the detachment as is, or as was, and we tried to use them to their maximum. The second reason why Major Tesic, Major Sljivancanin, did not have the authority to replace Mr. Jaksic lies in the fact that there has to be an order for any personnel-related issues. Tesic did not have the right to issue an order, a written order, a written document, relieving somebody of his duty, and in particular, he could not have had -- in particular, the assistant to the brigade commander, Major Sljivancanin, could not have had this kind of authority. In other words, the Operations Group was the level from which Captain Jaksic could be replaced, and there had to be a written order to that effect. Anything else simply brings me back to what I was talking about in the beginning. The jocular references, perhaps people saying jocularly, "Jaksic, you really need to be relieved of your duty." But mostly these remarks were made by people from his own detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we don't have Major Borivoje Tesic here. He testified before. But perhaps if we could give the English -- put the English version on the e-court, it's the same exhibit, L 0100531. This is an entry, page 36 of the English version. This is the entry in the war log for the 6th of November; the time is 1030. Did you find it? It's right there at the end of the page. I will read it now. "Village of Negoslavci, 1030, 6th of November. The commander of the Assault Detachment 1 reported that he had a problem with the engagement of part of a unit in combat (misunderstanding between members of volunteer units, Seselj's men and members of the TO). Remark, the column remark states that the commander of the Operations Group South ordered the Assault Detachment 1 to call and resolve the problems." Does this refer to what you were just testifying about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've just described the misunderstandings that would occur between them from time to time, and how we had to get involved in order for them to resolve those difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the testimony Major Tesic gave before the Court in Belgrade, he said that he had reported --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have an objection at this stage with regard to my learned friend leading on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: It is my understanding from the ruling made by this Chamber that co-defendants could not lead in such areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think I would expect it's the same thing. Are you objecting simply on the point of leading rather than having the witness give evidence of their own knowledge, or what is it that you're doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Certainly the witness can give evidence on his own knowledge, but the answer shouldn't be given to him in advance or anything suggested to him as to what Mr. Tesic has said from his testimony in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one question to clarify your previous answer. You said that Mr. Jaksic could be replaced only by the command of the Operations Group South, and my client was the security office chief in the Guards Brigade, which means that he would be a part of that command of Operations Group South. Who in the Operations Group South command could have made the decision to replace Mr. Jaksic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only Colonel Mile Mrksic, the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My last question. On the 19th, you were in the area where the hospital was. My question is: What was the situation on the access routes to the hospital in security terms and in the overall area, the bridges of the Vuka River, were you able to reach the hospital fairly easily or what was it like?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can describe this as follows: From the 10th of November, when our unit reached Milovo Brdo, until the 18th, from across the river Vuka and from all the buildings there, the Ministry of Interior, the Dunav hotel, the hospital and some other structures there, our unit was targeted at its positions in Milovo Brdo. Probably at that period, the Vuka River, its left bank, had been -- mines were laid there, because that was our assessment. All movements on the other bank of the Vuka River were -- was restricted to the bridge and one of the streets there, because we knew that this was the only route that could be used in light of the fact that all the other access routes were defended fiercely. That is why there was this dilemma and a great deal of caution from the evening of the 18th, throughout the night and in the morning of the 19th, how to get to the hospital. On the 19th, we used the road to get to the hospital. The reason for this was because we were afraid that in the side alleys and the areas between the houses, there would be mines. After the battle, it turned out that we were right, because the demining group found a certain number of anti-personnel mines in this area leading towards the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stijakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stijakovic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Serving as an officer in the Guards Motorised Brigade in Vukovar in 1991, is that something you're proud of?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an officer, I am very proud.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And very briefly, Mr. Stijakovic, can you tell us why serving with the Guards Motorised Brigade in Vukovar made you proud?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a very difficult, very big professional task together with my colleagues, and my superior command gave me this task and I carried it out successfully. Let me repeat: I did it in a professional manner, and the joy that I managed to perform this task, this is something that has to do solely with the professional side of this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And would part of your pride stem from the quality of the officers and the soldiers you were fighting with within the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, Mr. Stijakovic, about the role of the Guards Motorised Brigade and some of its functions before going to Vukovar with regard to guarding special facilities within former Yugoslavia, with regard to protecting the leaders of Yugoslavia, and with regard to visiting dignitaries. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: The higher echelon, the leaders of Yugoslavia who were being guarded by these people, they would not want to be guarded by cowards or ill-trained soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any leadership of any state in the world would deal with this issue in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And specifically what attributes did your officers and soldiers hold that made you proud?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to carry out our task in Vukovar in a situation in which the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, an internationally recognised state, was still whole, and every soldier in the army, on the basis of the tasks, the constitution and all the relevant legislation, was duty-bound to defend that country because, in one part of the country, there was armed rebellion and clashes in which paramilitary forces were involved. And to go on a mission in which you're supposed to defend your own country is something that every officer should consider as great honour. This is one of the reasons why an officer who performs such a mission feels so proud.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I could stop you there, Mr. Stijakovic, you're not actually answering the question you've been asked. What were the attributes of your soldiers and your fellow officers? Were they brave?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the soldiers and officers were brave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Were they dedicated?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Were they dedicated to the tasks they were performing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were disciplined and they performed tasks that were given to them, and I can assert that the factor of their determination, their will to perform the task, was in fact a key factor in the successful performance of their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: This Court has heard evidence, Mr. Stijakovic, that amongst soldiers of the Guards Motorised Brigade the fear was so palpable they had to be kept away from the front line. Is that true or is that a lie?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try not to interfere but the stage should be specified. We know this description. This was right at the start of the beginning, at the start of the operation in Vukovar, but to phrase it this way is highly leading and whimsical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, this is cross-examination. If the position is put on a false factual basis, the evidence is without merit. So I would propose to leave Mr. Lunny with his cross-examination without disruption on that basis. Carry on, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I could just ask you the question again, Mr. Stijakovic: This Court has heard evidence that the fear amongst soldiers of the Guards Motorised Brigade was so palpable they were kept away from the front line and direct combat. Is that the truth or is that a lie?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the Guards Brigade as a unit, and the composition of the Guards Brigade, this is not something that I can really evaluate. I can only talk about the soldiers that I had dealings with and these were the soldiers of the 1st Motorised Battalion. So that would be one-seventh of the Guards Brigade. When it comes to fear that you mentioned earlier, fear that the soldiers felt, let me tell you with complete honesty, I myself was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I could stop you there, Mr. Stijakovic. Again, you're not answering the question you've been asked. I'll rephrase it, given the first part of your answer. You can only speak about the 1st Motorised Battalion. With regard to the 1st Motorised Battalion, we've heard evidence that soldiers were so afraid they were kept away from the front line. Given what you've said about courage and dedication, is that statement the truth or is that statement a lie?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for individual soldiers, as for individual soldiers being afraid, they would tell their commanding officers very honestly and such soldiers were then removed to less important duties. Well, yes, there were soldiers who were afraid and who were removed from the actual front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And would the soldiers you're talking about be a whole company or just limited individuals?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking exclusively about individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You've told us several times yesterday about your own attributes, about how you were one of the best non-commissioned officers in the academy, a very good student, and a good teacher. And is it the case that you also excelled in your duties as Major Tesic's deputy?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said, when talking about myself, I did not say that I was excellent. I said that I was one of the best. As for what Major Tesic said about me during combat, or any one of my superiors, you should ask them about that. I cannot be so immodest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: In your own mind, did you perform your duties well in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think that I performed my duties well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: One of your duties was to deputise for the 1st Motorised Battalion when Tesic was away from the command post; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My duty was to deputise for him when he was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And having to deputise for the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion, you would have to be informed, equally well informed, of the situation around you with regards to the fighting and what was happening around Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My deputising for Major Tesic was exclusively in the zone and in the duties where he had command. As for the broader area, cooperation with neighbours, contacts with the superior command and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I could please stop you there, Mr. Stijakovic, and rephrase the question, then. With regard to the area for which you had responsibility, you had to keep yourself well informed of what was happening to be able to effectively deputise for Major Tesic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our area of responsibility, everything that happened there and that had to do with the implementation of our duties, yes, it is true. I had to be well aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Another duty for which you had responsibility was the keeping of the 1st Motorised Battalion war diary. And again, was that a duty you performed well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I performed that duty well. As for the diary, I recall that after combat action, when documents were being analysed in the superior command, Lieutenant-Colonel Trifunovic, the person in charge from the brigade command, pointed out that these documents were good and proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And in keeping the diary in a good and proper fashion, you must have been recording all the important events that occurred within your zone of responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for all events related to subordinate units that were recorded in the war diary, they were indeed recorded. They were indeed written down there. In addition to the war diary, there were a number of other documents that we kept there; namely, schematics, maps, plans of deployment, graphs and so on. So there were other documents that refer to what I spoke about a few moments ago; namely, the documents that Lieutenant-Colonel Trifunovic said were good.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Stijakovic, to perform that duty well, to keep the diary properly, you would need to be well informed of what was happening round about you within your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Events and knowledge was recorded in this diary, namely what we knew of. That means that it is an authentic recording of the knowledge that we had at the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Now, as well as the diary, you had other duties, including discipline for the battalion; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On orders from Major Tesic, I gave my contribution, in terms of disciplined conduct and the disciplined implementation of tasks received.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And again, was this a task you performed well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I performed that task well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: That task would again involve you being informed of what was happening round about you in the zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to be well informed as to what was happening in the zone, not round about. That is to say, in the zone of our responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Due to the death of a colleague before you left for Vukovar, you were also given responsibility for morale; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And as the officer in the 1st Motorised Battalion responsible for morale, was that a task you performed well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I performed that task in addition to my regular duties as deputy commander. I made an effort to do it as best I could. As for most of the work involved in carrying out that duty, namely as far as the battalion is concerned, it had to do with contacts with the media, that is to say people from that line of work who came in accordance with approval issued by the superior command. I was authorised to brief journalists about events that had to do with the 1st Battalion. As for the level of quality of this work done, again, I cannot say that it was high, but I made an effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And to make an effort as officer for morale, you would need to know how the men subordinated to you were feeling. You would need to know the mood of those men, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most responsible person for morale is the commander. Tesic was regularly informed about how the soldiers were doing, what the state of morale was, and he was the only person who had the right to issue orders on the basis of our proposals in order to maintain that state, improve it, and in order to prevent anything undesirable from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And you, being at the same command post as Major Tesic, you would be in receipt of the same information with regard to the state of morale, as you said?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for morale, we received the same information up to the 10th of November. From the 10th of November, Major Tesic, in addition to his regular duty as battalion commander, up to the 18th of November, led the remaining part of the 1st Assault Detachment. In that period, I could not be aware of the state that prevailed throughout all these units that he was in charge of. But specifically as for the 1st Motorised Battalion, yes, I had information throughout this period, from when we set out to carry out our task up until we were returning from having carried out our task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: The visit of Seselj to Vukovar and to men within your zone of responsibility was a significant incident, wasn't it, Mr. Stijakovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not an incident. That was a visit of a man, a person, who had his own party and a certain level of personnel that voluntarily took part in action. I repeat that that visit was not an incident. A -- it was a reminder. He came to see his own people, just like many other persons from other lines of work showed up in that zone. Specifically, I was -- I was visited by Mr. Saric, the director of Beteks, a major company from Belgrade. He brought some clothing to the front line for the men there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I could stop you there, Mr. Stijakovic, the question was in relation to Seselj only and his visit to troops within your zone of responsibility. You, as having a role in morale of the men, and knowing that the Leva Supoderica were Seselj's men, you would know that Seselj's visit would be good for their morale, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have only assumed that after his visit. I repeat: I did not know about the visit. It was only on the next day, once it had taken place, Lancuzanin told me about the visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And you, assuming that it was good for morale, no doubt would have approved of that visit, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not within my duties. The right or the possibility to grant permission for visits --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I could stop you there, Mr. Stijakovic, I wasn't asking you about what your duties were and what you could or could not grant permission for. I was asking for your view on Seselj's visit and the effect it would have on the morale of the men. You've agreed that you assumed it would be good for morale. And I'm asking you for your own opinion. Being the morale officer, you would have approved of that visit, then, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall repeat what I have said to you. I did not have the right to approve of that visit. If you're asking me now about my opinion regarding this visit, are you asking me about my present day opinion? You're asking about what I think today, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Does your view of the visit change between now and then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then, when the visit took place, I know that that visit contributed to that unit being involved with -- in carrying out this task with even greater responsibility. Was it because he addressed the units? What he did with them, what they talked about, that is something I don't know about. I, as a professional, was exclusively interested in the task that we had. If you're interested in what I think about it now, I assume that that has nothing to do with the events that are being considered here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You mentioned an address to the men and not knowing what was said. Is it your position, then, Mr. Stijakovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm following your instructions. This is already the third time that he is putting in different words what the witness said. This is not what the witness said. We have heard the continuity of his remarks. We can read all of this. This was too leading a question, in addition to everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't disagree with you, Mr. Borovic, but I would judge this witness well and truly capable of seeing if words are his words and evidence or not. So I don't think he needs to be protected. So carry on, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, at page 29, lines 4 into 5, you stated -- sorry, line 5: "What he did with them, what they talked about, that is something I don't know about." So you don't know what was said to the Leva Supoderica by Seselj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know what Mr. Vojislav Seselj said to his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: No one reported back to you after the Seselj visit that Seselj had stated not a single Ustasha must leave Vukovar alive?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not heard of such a statement before. This is the first time I hear about it, from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: So the second in command of the 1st Motorised Battalion, who has duties for a diary for which he needs information and needs to be well informed, who has duties for discipline for which he needs information and to be well informed, and who has responsibility or part responsibility for morale within the battalion and needs to know what is happening within the zone of responsibility, you heard absolutely nothing until today about that statement? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the statement that you presented before the Court a few moments ago, I first heard about it from you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may be an appropriate point for the morning break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 20 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, can the witness please have before him Exhibit 409, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, this is an order of 19th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to raise an objection, but think I'll give this particular objection up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, you're very understanding. We will use that as a model for all future objections in the mind of all counsel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Do you see that order in front of you, Mr. Stijakovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I do. But not so clearly, if that could please be blown up a little. That's okay now. It's perfect now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can I refer you -- sorry, before I do so, this is an order from Lieutenant-General Zivota Panic of 19th of November to a number of bodies, including Operations Group South, and you were in Operations Group South on the 19th of October, 1991. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order is dated the 19th of October, 1991, on which day I was a member of the 1st Motorised Battalion. Through the command of the 1st Assault Detachment, this was effectively part of Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And can you look, please, at numbered paragraph 4 in that order? It's page 3 on the English translation, Your Honour. And in the second page of the B/C/S. Could you please read out paragraph 4 for us, Mr. Stijakovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In order to prevent looting, mistreatment of civilians, and" -- can't quite make out the following word, "mistreatment of civilians and" -- it goes on, "even prisoners, all armed persons and groups not a part of the JNA or TO, Chetniks and such-like, shall be disarmed and detained while their leaders shall be locked up with legal steps being taken against them."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. -- rather, Mr. Stijakovic, the word that you couldn't read on the first line, is it not "murder"? And the statement reads: "In order to prevent looting, the abuse" --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Mistreatment of civilians," that is possible, yes, "murder." I couldn't quite make out the first two letters but that is a distinct possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Were you aware of that order when it was issued in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had this order not been issued, we were doing all these things any way. I suppose this is a result of information and indication that there were things like this going on in certain areas. As for the 1st Assault Detachment, or rather the 1st Motorised Battalion, on the date you specified there were no such things happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But in any event, as early as 19th of October, 1991, you were aware of potential for mistreatment and murder of detained persons; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. By Your Honours' leave, I can describe for your benefit our experience with prisoners. This occurred on the second night of the fighting, as early as the 2nd of October. The first person that was captured, this person was armed. He was a member of the paramilitary units. He was captured in the area of operations of Captain Zirojevic's company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can I stop you there, Mr. Stijakovic? I wasn't asking you about a specific incident on a specific time, but I'm asking you about what information you had in October 1991 with regard to the possible risk of mistreatment and murder of detained persons and this order from Zivota Panic warning of such mistreatment, and is it not the case that the 1st Motorised Battalion, yourself and Major Tesic and everyone else within OG South, was fully aware of the risk to detained, captured prisoners from the other side? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We bore that danger in mind throughout. We always tried to do whatever we could under the law to take steps to ensure this didn't happen. What I tried to tell you a while ago, I tried to describe for you the capture of this paramilitary person, in order to describe our firmest conviction to act very strictly and in a very professional manner --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Could I stop you --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness please be allowed to finish his answers? My colleague seems to have gotten into the rut of cutting him off in midstream, whereas I think it would only be fair for the witness to be allowed to finish his answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could Mr. Stijakovic now have before him Exhibit 415, please. And if I can direct the registrar to the last page of the document, page 4 of the English translation, and in particular paragraph number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can you please read out paragraph number 8 for us, Mr. Stijakovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Each unit in its own area of responsibility must establish full control over the overall situation in the territory. The commanders at all levels shall henceforth be responsible for this. The laws of war have not taken effect yet. By the same token, and anyway, no one has the right to any acts of retaliation or other forms of revenge, such as those committed by certain local units of the TO. Any such future actions shall see their perpetrators arrested with legal action being brought against them."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, this is an order again from General Zivota Panic. It's now the 18th of November. It's a month later. And it's a very similar warning to, amongst others, Operations Group South, to be particularly aware of retribution carried out to people within the area. Again, this is something you were aware of, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat that this order, as well as the previous one, did not bring anything new that we, in our area of responsibility, the area of responsibility of the 1st Motorised Battalion, were not doing already. I repeat: Throughout our time in the area that was assigned to us, we were in full control of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Now, you say you were in full control of the situation. The first order from 19th of October is a warning. The second document, a month later, refers to retribution and revenge which some local TO units carried out, and "carried out" is in the past tense, meaning that retribution and other kinds of revenge have actually taken place. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of no such acts of retaliation or retribution. There was no retaliation in the area covered by the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, you were in charge of the diary. You were in charge of discipline. You had responsibilities for morale. You told us you had to be well informed or informed. It's your position that you knew nothing of any such acts between mid-October and mid-November?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of no such acts committed in the area of responsibility of my unit. There were no such acts committed, nor was I aware of anything like that occurring in the general area. We were a small unit, that's true, and we covered a relatively limited area. As for what was going on outside that area in Operations Group South, Operations Group North, and other parts of the front is not something that I was able to ascertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: This small area that you had command for included Nova Ulica street, didn't it? You're nodding, Mr. Stijakovic. If you please answer verbally, so it's recorded.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nova Ulica was part of our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And Nova Ulica was close to where your headquarters were, Svetozara Markovica street; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nova Ulica was close to the HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: This Court has heard evidence of killings taking place in a house opposite 81 Nova Ulica street, and you, being the officer for the diary and discipline and morale, were fully aware of what was going on in Nova Ulica street, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew nothing of any killings at Nova street. First I hear of it, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: The Leva Supoderica, Petrova Gora and the TO volunteers who were fighting within your zone of responsibility were fighting for their own homes and their villages and towns, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What were the motives for the combat involvement of the Leva Supoderica Detachment or the Petrova Gora Detachment? Were they fighting for their own personal profit? This is not really something that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But the battle-ground that you found yourself in within OG South and Vukovar, that contained the area of Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora and units from those members were fighting with you and under you and they were fighting to liberate their home town and their own houses and their own people, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the units, some of the troops from the Leva Supoderica unit did indeed hail from the area. There were members of that unit who had joined voluntarily, who hailed from other areas as well, who weren't locals. Both units had within their composition people who were outside Vukovar -- from outside Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Members of the Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica were based in and around Nova Ulica, Leva Supoderica street and Svetozara Markovica street, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You specified the locations of these detachments. Some of those units were indeed deployed the way you've just suggested. However, these are places where these units stayed, slept or rested. But it was from there that they would join battle in an organised manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But they stayed, slept and rested in very close proximity to your headquarters, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat this for you: The area in which a combat task was carried out was a relatively small area but it was a built-up area, populated area, with many houses and many buildings. So under the weather conditions that prevailed at the time, it was only natural for people to take shelter in houses, shelter from the elements and precipitations. It was much in the same way that the Leva Supoderica Detachment was for the most part in various houses in Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora. As for the other one that you mentioned, Leva Supoderica people were mostly in the Leva Supoderica district. It is true that, geographically speaking, these areas were in close physical proximity to our command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You also mentioned yesterday at page 63 in your transcript a great concentration of different people, civilians, people that were moving around, people that lived in that area. So as well as the Petrova Gora and other volunteers and TO detachments, there were civilians staying nearby your headquarters within the Petrova Gora neighbourhood; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were whole families living in some of the houses, some families that just happened to be there when the fighting erupted and were in no position to leave. Likewise, our own host, Mr. Jagetic and his wife Dubravka, were spending most of their time in an outbuilding that was located next to our own headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Stijakovic, that after the fall of Vukovar, on the 18th of November, you left to return to Belgrade on the 24th of November; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the liberation of Vukovar, and the surrender of the paramilitary units from the 18th of November onwards, we were carrying out preparations pursuant to orders from our superior command, and eventually on the 24th we returned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And in that period between the 18th and right up to the 24th, you were still based at Petrova Gora, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ever since our arrival in the town, and I'm talking about our HQ, we stayed at Svetozara Markovica street and that's where we left when we were off to Belgrade. What I mean is that the HQ never moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And indeed on the 19th of November, your direct superior, Major Tesic, was appointed the Petrova Gora commander, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Major Tesic, pursuant to orders of the superior command, was the person responsible for the area. This area can be indicated on a map, if necessary. He was the person responsible to his own superior, the commander of Operations Group, for everything. He was to make sure that there was order and discipline in the area, and Tesic was the most responsible person. And this area covered part of the Petrova Gora area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Could the witness please have before him Exhibit 418? Excuse me, Your Honour. Would Your Honour please bear with me for just a moment? Just checking the exact reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, is it not the case that on the 19th of November Tesic was appointed the town commander for Petrova Gora? If you just allow me a moment. Could you please look to paragraph 4 on page 2, Mr. Stijakovic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I read this out, paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If you would, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "During the day, three members of our unit were pulled out from the hospital."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I could stop you there, I think it's the wrong reference. I do apologise, Mr. Stijakovic. It's page 2, paragraph 4 in the English translation, Your Honour. I do apologise for this. There appears to be two paragraph 4s on page 2. It's further up the page.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, is that the one you want me to read out?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Yes, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Now that Vukovar has been liberated, the following persons have been appointed commanders. For Vucedol and Mitnica, Major Miroslav Stupar. For Petrova Gora and the area to the west of the cemetery and as far as the Vuka River, Major Borivoje Tesic. For the area between Sajmiste street and the area east of Mitnica, Major Adem Bajic. At one point in time, during the day, the tactical group of the 195th Motorised Brigade joined the composition of OG South. This element" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, the rest of the paragraph we don't need to hear. But from that document is it not clear that Major Borivoje Tesic was appointed town commander for Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is patently clear based on this order that Major Tesic was the komandant of the area in which we operated. Again, if you'd like me to, I can mark that for you on a map. The settlement of Petrova Gora lies within the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: During this time from 18th to the 24th of November, you were based in Petrova Gora, your direct superior is the commander, town commander of Petrova Gora, you are surrounded by the civilians of Petrova Gora, you have members of Petrova Gora TO living in houses nearby your command post, and from the 20th of November to the 24th in particular, you hear nothing about the deaths of 260 people within the farm at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Back in 1995, I hadn't yet heard about 200-something persons having been killed at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday it wasn't until 1995 that you found out about these deaths at Ovcara farm.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. And as I repeated a while ago, I first heard of Ovcara as a concept back in 1995 in the public media. I happened to be in Banja Luka at the time I heard this. This was the very first time I heard that proceedings had been instituted and that a number of officers were suspected of that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And the officers suspected and later some convicted in Belgrade, some of those convicted persons came from the Petrova Gora Detachment, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the Belgrade Ovcara trial, I know that a trial was held, whether this year or last year. And what I also know is that Major Tesic appeared as a witness. I was never summoned by the Court to speak about that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: This Court has heard evidence that the killings at Ovcara were reported as early as 1992. It's still your position that you remained ignorant of all of these deaths for a further three years?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is still my position, and for the umpteenth time I say that I only heard about this event in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Is it not the case, Mr. Stijakovic, that from the morning of 21st November, in the last few days that you were at Vukovar, that everyone in the town was talking about the deaths that had occurred at Ovcara farm? Civilians were talking about them, Petrova Gora, Leva Supoderica, people involved in those killings were going around the streets talking about what had happened, and you, as the officer of the 1st Motorised Battalion, responsible for keeping information in the diary, responsible for knowing information for disciplinary purposes, as an officer responsible for morale of those within your zone of responsibility, it is in fact the case that you heard those rumours and knew very well that those deaths had occurred back in November 1991, from the 21st of November onwards?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The period that you mentioned, from the 19th until the 24th, is the period in which I, together with Major Tesic and the company commanders, focused our activities on the regular troops that we had brought in from Belgrade to the war zone. And we had so many things to do, from the equipment, to the ammunition and weapons that were issued to them, the fact that some of the weapons were rusty, the equipment was out of order, mortars were damaged, the vehicles were not functioning, the clothes were strewn all over the place, so many problems that oppressed a professional officer, and the task was also sometime ahead to bring that all back. Imagine what it is like when you're responsible for a single pistol being lost, and here you're talking about a situation where loads of weapons were being lost. All my energy was focused on this issue, and I can state that I really did not have any contacts with any civilian structures from the 18th onwards because the fact that the city had been liberated was a great event for everyone. My hosts disappeared. Dubravka left in search of her father who had been killed at Mitnica, who was at the other side of the front line. So everybody was focused on performing tasks that were important for them, and my task was as I have just described to you, so that I could not have heard or I could not have participated in any discussions of the -- of this crime. And as an officer, I can be held responsible by my superior and to tell him why I didn't know something, but when I say that I didn't know, I didn't know. I only learned about that in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I'll move on to a new topic, Mr. Stijakovic. Yesterday, at page 74 in your evidence, you said that there were problems with cooperation between battalion and the TO detachments. Can you please give us some examples of the problems with cooperation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how should I put it? These are just run-of-the-mill problems one encounters in one's work. If you're a businessman today, you encounter all kinds of problems, and the same goes for this situation. This is a specific situation where you have people working, people living there, and problems are inevitable. I can share my experience with you, the first -- my first meeting with the people that lived there, how the problems simply grew.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I can stop you there. If you could please do that, then, Mr. Stijakovic. I was afraid you were beginning to go off on a tangent with regard to business relationships. But what were the difficulties, then, with cooperation with the people who were there, particularly between the battalion and the TO detachments, as you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like you to show me that. The problems that I talked about yesterday could only be of this nature. These are the problems involving cooperation, mutual support, problems related to the evacuation of the wounded and the sick, the freedom of movement within the zone. So those are the problems that were encountered every day, and at that level of cooperation, and acting in concert, we solved them as we went along. So I would like you to tell me what specific problem you want me to respond to, what did you want to ask me about? What specific problem? And then I will try to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned problems with cooperation between battalion and TO detachments and that this resulted in the order of 29th of October bringing the Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora and TO detachment under the 1st Motorised Battalion and under Captain Tesic. You mentioned there problems with mutual support. Can you tell us what do you mean by "problems with mutual support"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The execution of any mission or action had to be prepared well, in light of the quality of our enemy, the support they had, the fire that they would open on us. The problems occurred because nobody could force anybody to take up his rifle the next day and head down Nova Ulica street towards the mini market. There had to be a certain amount of determination for a subgroup or group to implement the plan that had been drawn up. That means that there were situations in which a subgroup belonging to the Leva Supoderica Detachment disagreed or simply did not want to take the axis that we had envisaged, and then you have to go over the plan again and then it's a long process before all those elements of the combat disposition are brought where they have to be and the task is performed. These are the problems that you encounter where you have human beings trying to reach an agreement and then sometimes they are willing to do some things, at other times they are unwilling, then somebody claims he's tired, and that is why we had to analyse those problems day in, day out, make plans, and then we had to implement those plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Is it the case, then, that the original setup you described yesterday, with the TO and other volunteer detachments fighting alongside in cooperation with the JNA army, with the 1st Motorised Battalion, simply wasn't working?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
