utterances.text: It did function, but it required proper preparation, planning and execution of tasks. This means acting in concert, all those structures acting in concert in the performance of all the tasks such as the liberation of the mini market, the "seste proleterske divisije," Milovo Brdo, and once this team was -- started functioning well, everything was fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But you told us yesterday, Mr. Stijakovic, on the 29th of October, the structure was changed on account of problems with cooperation between battalion and TO detachments. Can you give us some further examples of what those problems were?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to respond to your question in this way. This was not a private war in which every unit would do only those things that were in its interest. It is quite logical that the volunteer forces, or, rather, I apologise, members of the Territorial Defence, should be grouped together in such a way that we, the JNA units, and we the JNA officers led them, lest we should find ourselves in a situation in those decisive days of the battle, people who would be exercising command as they saw fit. So the decision of the superior command to group all those units in a single whole is just an expression of the focus. Focus is a military term. It means that at a certain front, the focus is something which is where you concentrate your forces and your support, and our command decided that the focus should be on the 1st Motorised Battalion, and as for the -- and then, in fact, the 1st Assault Detachment, and the 1st detachment commander decided that the 3rd Motorised Company should be on the focus, which means that Captain Miroslav Radic had this role. And that is how all this was decided. Our intention to make a winning team out of all those units was the result of this decision to turn them all into military units, lest there should be any actions that would be outside of any control or result of somebody's own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You mentioned that the 3rd Motorised Company should be on the focus with Captain Radic in this role. Was this partly because -- this was because of Captain Radic's personality and command he held with the soldiers? He was respected and they followed him; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two reasons why this focus was selected. The first is the result of the study of the situation on the enemy lines. We, in our detachment, realised that it would be best to liberate the town, that we would do it the fastest if we took Milovo Brdo. We also knew that if we cut the Bogdanovci road, then the paramilitary forces would find themselves completely encircled, and from Nova Ulica to mini market there were just a couple of hundred metres. That is the first reason why the focus for the deployment of the unit was reassigned to the left wing of our unit. The second reason is that this is where the Leva Supoderica Detachment and the Petrova Gora Detachment and Captain Radic were located there. They were preparing for their engagements there. And there was also Captain Radic, who had already shown his mettle in previous engagements. These were the reasons that led us to refocus the deployment of our unit to Bogdanovci to the Prvog Maja street and to get to Milovo Brdo as soon as possible. Milovo Brdo was a strategic feature in the battle for the city of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And in that group that you've described with Captain Radic and the Leva Supoderica and the Petrova Gora, he was the only professional officer within that group, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Lieutenant Elvir Hadzic was also a professional officer in his unit. There was also Sergeant Jovanovic. He had fallen ill. And there was also (redacted), who was his company NCO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there as professional officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But Captain Radic was the most senior professional officer amongst those men and therefore also amongst the Leva Supoderica, Petrova Gora, and the volunteers, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every 24 hours, there were two stages, or two parts of this relationship. Please allow me to explain how Captain Radic was, in fact -- in what sense he was the most responsible person there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: So you're agreeing with me, Mr. Stijakovic, that Captain Radic was indeed the most senior and the most responsible person within the group you've described?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the assault group, which is a temporary formation, which in 24 hours, as a temporary formation, in most instances was active from 8.00 a.m. until, let's say, 1500 to 1600 hours, this temporary formation had its subgroups in accordance with the task ahead for that day. And it is true that on the part of the superior command, Major Tesic, myself, that the best person to command this temporary formation, the assault group, was Captain Miroslav Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You've described this as a temporary formation, Mr. Stijakovic. That's not true, is it? This relationship was set up and continued until the 21st of November, 1991; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That is not true. If the Honourable Chamber allows me to explain how this temporary formation carried out its tasks, and once I do that, it will be clear to you. Let me repeat: A temporary formation functioned only in combat, or any other active tasks, movement and so on. Once the action was finished, then soldiers who were less able are brought to the line that had been attained. Guards are put there, and this whole area is guarded against any possible attempts of the opposite side to retake it. And the assault group, all its members, go back to their original units to rest. This means that this temporary formation, once it's liberated Milovo Brdo, ceased exist de facto and de jure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: That's different from what you said yesterday, Mr. Stijakovic, isn't it? Yesterday you described the 1st Motorised Battalion as the most able, as the most successful, and after they had reached their target, from the 10th to the 18th, they were left to control the ground taken, and now you're telling us that the less able ones, the less able soldiers, are sent to carry out that task. Which one is correct, Mr. Stijakovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I spoke about the 1st Motorised Battalion and the 1st Assault Detachment, and I explained how those two units were split apart after the 10th of November and also what happened after the 14th of November, and now I want to explain to you about the temporary formation that is called an assault group. The assault group commanded on the focus of the action by Captain Radic was a temporary formation composed of the bravest and best soldiers, and I can tell you the following. When this assault group is deployed and when it liberates, for instance, Bosko Buha neighbourhood, from 1400 hours, 1500, 1600 hours, once the task is over, the assault group withdraws into the depth of the territory to Leva Supoderica, Nova Ulica, whatever, and the line that was attained is then guarded by less able soldiers. I now explained to you the functioning of the assault group commanded by Miroslav Radic until the 10th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You've told us -- you told the Court, Mr. Stijakovic, about this division between the 1st Motorised Battalion and the 1st Assault Detachment, and it starts with an oral order of Major Tesic on the 12th of November; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Tesic issued an order, oral order, on the 12th of November relaying an order received from Mile Mrksic on the separation of the 1st Assault Detachment and the 1st Motorised Battalion, or, to be more specific, ordering that the 1st Motorised Battalion be taken out of the composition of the 1st Assault Detachment. This oral order of the 12th of November was then turned into a written order that reached our unit on the 14th of November and we had the opportunity to see it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, could you please look at Exhibit 401 for me? It is the diary of the Guards Motorised Brigade, war diary. And for the B/C/S version of this exhibit, would you please look, first of all, at 02935475? And in the English translation, L 0100532. You've told us the oral order came, first of all, from Mrksic to Tesic. Can you please show us in Exhibit 401 where that oral order is referred to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the war log kept by the superior command, so this oral order that I'm talking to you about can only be -- its existence can only be proven through witness testimony, but in the actual fact, the order issued on the 14th covers all that. I don't know anything about the contents of this war log because some other person kept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of witness testimony about this oral order, are you -- you've told us already, Mr. Stijakovic, that Major Tesic gave evidence in the Belgrade trial; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard, and I read in the media, that Major Tesic had testified before the Court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: At no time in the course of his testimony in Belgrade did he ever mention an oral order of the 12th of November. Can you please comment on that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The oral order that was -- that later on took the form of a written order has no significance. Therefore, Major Tesic received his written order on the 14th to act in accordance with the oral order, which means that, that an introduction to the 14th of November dated the 12th of November can be accepted or not, but the written order confirmed the state of affairs and that is that from then on, the 1st Motorised Battalion would no longer be part of the 1st Assault Detachment. I am testifying about what I heard on the 12th, but it has no such weight as the written order that you were able to see yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Major Tesic also gave three statements in Belgrade prior to testimony, and again in none of those statements did he ever mention an order of the 12th of November. He further gave a statement to the ICTY, to the Office of the Prosecutor, and again, he made no reference to this oral order of the 12th of November. This order didn't happen, did it, Mr. Stijakovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That order did happen, and this oral order, by way of an introduction, I can say that it was a process that was prepared from the 10th of November, when already in the evening, on the basis of company commanders, our subordinates, we heard their views regarding further activity. Each and every one of them presented their position, that, having reached Milovo Brdo, they completed their combat activity, that they were exhausted and tired, that it was only logical that other detachments and other battalions should carry out their tasks. And I assume that Mr. Tesic did not talk about that anywhere because, in a way, that briefing had displayed the feeling that existed among the subordinates that, as for future tasks, there is not the kind of will that existed up until the 10th of November. What ensued was a process of accommodating this kind of feeling within the unit, and trying to find a solution by way of bridging the problem that occurred. It was only logical for it to have been written the way it was on the 14th of November. The 1st Battalion had completed its combat activity. We were extremely grateful, all the company commanders and I, to our superior command for having exempted us from --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You're coming away from the original question which was the existence or otherwise of this oral order of the 12th. Can I now refer you, please, to your own diary? It should be in e-court, Your Honour, under Y 0079884 to Y 0079894. Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Stijakovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you just ask for it to be enlarged, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You made reference to this document yesterday in your examination-in-chief, Mr. Stijakovic, with regard to keeping a copy of this after you returned from Vukovar to Belgrade. And is this the document we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a copy that was written by soldier Dobras, my messenger, and I was the one who dictated the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday, Mr. Stijakovic, that the purpose behind this was for scientific research and military research so that when the time was right you could write about Vukovar and the battle for Vukovar; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My intention was, and it still exists, in relation to this part of my statement that I'm proud of, I wished to transform this into useful material for officer training as to fighting in built-up areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And in that regard, you would then be careful to retain all the important information from that diary when you made the copy, information that you could then pass on as part of that training, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I selected the content regarding each and every day, the content that I assessed that I could use later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And the change in formation that you have described on the 12th of November with this oral order, that was something that you would select as being important, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that change of formation, now that we are talking about the 12th, it was actually more important as far as the 10th of November was concerned, as I said I described or only pinpointed those occurrences that had to do with tactics, where activity takes place, where certain features are reached, those that involve deaths and injuries, because I wished to make a comparison between activities and possible casualties, human losses. With your permission, it was my claim and still is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, you've mentioned the information you wanted to retain. The order of the 12th that followed from the change on the 10th is a significant incident, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall repeat: An oral order --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: No, no, please don't repeat your answer. I'm asking you a specific question in relation to the oral order of the 12th and the change in the disposition of the 1st Motorised Battalion and the 1st Assault Detachment, as you described yesterday. Was that or was that not an important incident or decision? And the answer to that question is yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The change of the 14th of November is important. The 12th was a preceding one. It was only conveyed orally. The 14th is the most important because there is material evidence. There is a document stating that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: The purpose of this diary was for your thesis for training. We are talking about the last week in the fight for Vukovar and how troops are divided or not divided, and how they are used in this those last few days of Vukovar was of crucial importance, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And the timings of any resubordination or changes or use of troops would be important as well, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, important, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And the actual physical change or movement or resubordination, that would be more significant than any follow-up written order; the actual change itself, if one took place, would be more significant than anything in writing, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can I ask you, then, please to look at your diary, this record that was going to be used for this thesis of yours? And will you look at page 9893 in the B/C/S, please, and the entries dealing with the 10th to the 12th of November? It's on page 9 of the English translation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I read the entry of the 10th of November or the last sentence of that particular entry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to read out the entries. I want you to find on that page, on the 10th, 11th, or 12th, if there is any reference to any oral order from Major Tesic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not mentioned in these writings. But I asked you for permission for me to read out the last sentence of the 10th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: That's not necessary, Mr. Stijakovic. We have your answer. On the 10th, 11th, or 12th there is no mention of any oral order having been issued. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a few moments ago that I am proving this assertion through my own testimony. As for writings, this oral order is not in this copy of mine where already on the 12th these two units are being separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You mentioned this separation of the 1st Assault Detachment and the 1st Motorised Battalion. Isn't it the case that there was in fact no separation and that the troops who were under Captain Radic, the Leva Supoderica and the Petrova Gora, were not moved in any way, shape or form by that written order of the 14th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that the separation followed from the evening of the 10th onwards, and I assert that from that evening onwards, the company commanders, Captain Radic, Zirojevic and Bojkovski, asked that their further military engagement should stop. That separation was certainly carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time is just leaving 20 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's probably a convenient time, is it, Mr. Lunny?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: It is, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, though, thinks you need more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't think that. Your Honour, could I just clarify one or two small matters? It's quite simply this. I know there is another witness to follow, but I wonder if my learned friend could assist whether in actual fact it is his hope to have two witnesses today and tomorrow or just one? Because there is one small problem. Your Honour may remember that we had sought to introduce three of the -- what I will call alibi witnesses, and unfortunately the waivers seem to have been delayed. They now have been served. The one witness is here, and Mr. Weiner was hoping to interview him. We received a briefing note which tends to change matters somewhat, and it's really a case of trying to work out and coordinate time. That's the first point. The second point relates to Mr. Sljivancanin. It may well be that the case for Mr. Radic will conclude perhaps on Tuesday or Wednesday, perhaps with the exception of the expert and that has to be clarified. Would it be the Court's intention, indeed Mr. Lukic's intention to commence Mr. Sljivancanin, let us say, on Thursday rather than waste time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: From the point of view of the Chamber, we would expect to move on to the evidence to be led by Mr. Lukic at the end of the case for Mr. Radic. Whether in the course of the evidence now being led by Mr. Borovic we will reach not just one but a second further witness in the course of today and tomorrow, time will tell. I anticipate that if Mr. Borovic had any problem with a witness being available, he would indicate that. And we do know that next week, among the witnesses to follow in Mr. Borovic's case, is an expert who is anticipated to take a longer time than the other witnesses. Would you at this moment, Mr. Borovic, be able to estimate when your case might finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this significantly depends on the effectiveness of the Prosecution, and it's nothing to write home about based on what we've heard today. Then we will have a problem. I examined my two witnesses according to my plan. If that plan is observed, in accordance with the time limits set, then everything will be the way we presented it to the Trial Chamber. My next witness is prepared to take the stand today. That's all I have to say. As for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To the end of your case, Mr. Borovic, is it to be Wednesday or Thursday of next week, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, one witness is planned for Monday, another one for Tuesday, and the expert at the end, Wednesday or Thursday. That, of course, is the end. That is before the 20th of October, as you had planned. Since the Prosecution is worried about whether they can interview my witnesses during the weekend, they can. I don't mind them interviewing all my witnesses, and I'm stating that yet again, now, in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're already anticipating me. Is it convenient to you to start your evidence before that long weekend that we have or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally would not like that. It actually depends on how much time we have left next week. If it's only one day, I would kindly ask that we start on Wednesday. I mean, possibly I could do my opening statement, but I would like to do a bit more work with Mr. Sljivancanin, and Monday and Tuesday would really be important for me. I wouldn't like the testimony to start because then I cannot contact him any longer. Yesterday I got over 1.000 pages of material, and I'll say that quite openly, from the OTP and it has to do with my client, and I already discussed this with Mr. Moore. It has to do with questions that they want to put to my client. I'm afraid that if they start showering me with these documents, some of which are quite new, then I really have to deal with them before that. I know that Mr. Sljivancanin is going to say that he is prepared to testify straight away, but I, as his Defence counsel, would really like him to start on the 25th, as envisaged, and that's what I said to my witnesses, that that would be the time frame for their arrivals, and I will strictly abide by the guidelines set for my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good. As long as by starting on the 25th we can be sure of finishing on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's, we feel, too early at the moment to make a firm direction. If there are two days of evidence available next week, I think we should press on, and it should be borne in mind that we will have longer sitting days on Tuesday and Wednesday of next week, trying to get as much time as possible for -- to assist the Defence in the presentation of its case. But if the evidence should slow down during Mr. Borovic's case, and you're really hemmed into the Friday, Mr. Lukic, you may find our hearts soften. But I would at the moment plan on the basis that the greater likelihood is that we will conclude Mr. Borovic's evidence and be ready for you by Thursday. Today, I think it would be convenient, because we are a little later than expected breaking, if we did not resume until 10 past 2.00, and we will adjourn now until then. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: In the course of your evidence yesterday, Mr. Stijakovic, you told the Court that: "Up to the 18th of November, the whole battalion, not only the company, remained at Milovo Brdo, deployed according to companies from that sector, our units did not take a single step from there." Are you then saying that from the 10th until the 18th, the 1st Motorised Battalion did not move from Milovo Brdo and did not take part in combat activities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 1st Motorised Battalion was not involved --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered the question with a yes. Can you please now look at your diary again, Y 0079884 to Y 0079894, and in particular at pages 10 and 11 in the B/C/S, and pages 9 and 10 in the English translation. If I can start with the 10th of November, please, Mr. Stijakovic, it states: "On the basis of the previous plan of attack, the battalion carried out an action and captured Milovo Brdo." So you're fighting still on the 10th, that's correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The fighting continued until the afternoon on the 14th and our unit reached Milovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Stop. You answered it with a yes, that's correct. But you've told us that from the 10th until the 18th the battalion was not involved in military actions or combat. Can you now please look at the entry for the 13th of November? "In the course of the day, the battalion carried out offensive actions and captured the neighbourhood itself at the foot-hills of Milovo Brdo." That entry, Mr. Stijakovic, contradicts your evidence yesterday, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You told us yesterday between the 10th and the 18th there was no combat, and yet your diary says on the 13th there was combat. Can you please explain why that is so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of November, our unit reached Milovo Brdo. Having reached Milovo Brdo, the firing as well as the involvement of the 1st Motorised Battalion stopped. This means that by the 10th of November, we had managed to liberate the Milovo Brdo area itself. Milovo Brdo is a geographical concept. There are streets there descending towards the downtown area and the Vuka River. Given the fact that our orders on further action said, "Be at the ready for any further action," the unit commanders, in order to reinforce the lines reached up until that point, took action in the Milovo Brdo area. Therefore, this entry is merely in relation to reinforcing the lines already reached by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You are entry for the 13th of November does not use the word "reinforce" anywhere; isn't that correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that the word "reinforce" is not used. But, on the other hand, you have an action described there which means precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell the Court, Mr. Stijakovic, that the phrase "offensive actions" is the equivalent of "reinforcement"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Reinforcing any lines reached might also comprise offensive actions. This is an action carried out by a small group of people who in order to fortify any lines reached may decide to move forwards or backwards, left or right, but only small distances, such as the hundred of metres specified in this particular entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, if we can now look at the entry for the 17th of November. "The battalion today organised an attack and entered the very centre of Vukovar." Again, Mr. Stijakovic, you told the Court yesterday that up until the 18th, you were not -- the battalion was not involved in combat operations. Do you agree that this entry shows that the battalion was very much involved in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th, the battalion entered Vukovar's downtown area. We liberated the first bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Please stop, Mr. Stijakovic. The answer to the question should be yes or no. I don't want you to describe what happened or what fighting took place. The question was: On the 17th of November, were you still involved in combat operations, the 1st Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The 1st Motorised Battalion was active from Milovo Brdo on the 17th as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: We also see in the entry of the 17th, the use of the word "detachment." You've given an explanation about the division of the 1st Assault Detachment earlier that week, the 1st Motorised Battalion holding Milovo Brdo and the assault detachment fighting elsewhere. Is it not then the case on the 17th of November the 1st Assault Detachment was back together with the rest of the 1st Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th, the 1st Assault Detachment was not recorded, at least as far as I can tell by looking at my own entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You do say on the 17th of November, Mr. Stijakovic: "We had six wounded members of the detachment in these battles." You're referring to the same battles that the 1st Motorised Battalion is engaged in, and you use the word "we," meaning soldiers subordinated to you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a reference in relation to the 1st Motorised Battalion, and obviously it has to do with the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Do you agree, though, Mr. Stijakovic, that you used the word "detachment" in that paragraph? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The entry says "detachment" but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you've answered the question with a yes. You do refer to the detachment on the 17th of November. I want to ask you now about the issue of tasks. In the course of your evidence yesterday, you mentioned carrying out tasks on a number of occasions. And is it the case that a task is simply a definite goal, something to be achieved, and you had given an order to carry out that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assignment mentioned yesterday has an objective, a final objective, and this assignment is issued because of this objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And different tasks, Mr. Stijakovic, would involve different numbers of men; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Different tasks involve different numbers of men, and the equipment also varies according to each task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can you now please look at Exhibit 420 -- sorry, 430, Mr. Stijakovic? And if you look at, please, paragraph 4, at the foot of page 1 in the B/C/S version, and paragraph 4 on page 2 of the English version. As I understand it from yesterday, and from your evidence yesterday, it was your position that this order removed the TO Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora who were at that time acting under Captain Radic and then subordinated them directly to Major Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were continually subordinated to Major Tesic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note we are not sure we got the answer right because there was overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, you do not interrupt the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is it that you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I want to say is that I believe my learned friend might use some preparation for this trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: It was your position earlier this morning, Mr. Stijakovic, that Captain Radic was the highest professional soldier within the assault groups, and that under Captain Radic, he had command of the Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: The order of the 14th, Exhibit 430, refers to regrouping. There is no reference anywhere in that order to resubordination; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question for me? And what exactly is that supposed to be in reference to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: The order, Exhibit 430, which you have said divided up the 1st Assault Detachment from the 1st Motorised Battalion at no time mentions resubordination but only refers to regrouping; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the detachment, you mean? Yes. It is true that the order separates --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There is no reference to resubordination. The order then continues to provide tasks, or a task, for the 1st Assault Detachment without the 1st Motorised Battalion; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was. The assignments were received by the assault detachment separately and the 1st Motorised Battalion for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And isn't it true, Mr. Stijakovic, that this order of the 14th of November was simply issuing a specific task to be carried out by a specific number of men who then returned to the 1st Motorised Battalion, the 1st Assault Detachment came back together before the 17th of November as is reflected in your diary?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You wouldn't allow me to explain the entry dated the 17th, what it means, the reference to the six wounded soldiers from the detachment. By the Chamber's leave, I would like to explain that, and then I will move on to the other question too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 17th of November, six wounded members of the detachment of the neighbouring unit were taken in an ambulance back to positions held by our own forces and they were taken to the collection site in the hospital itself. This entry is only in reference to activities that had to do with assisting one of the adjacent units. Therefore, the separation that we are looking at, a separation of these two units, was solely in reference to active movement and active assignments between the 14th and the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, if you again look back at your diary, and on page 11 of the B/C/S and page 10 of the English, the entry for the 17th of November makes no reference to neighbouring detachment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six wounded soldiers, members of the detachment. This is the neighbouring unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, you're not answering the question you've been asked, which is the entry of the 17th of November makes no reference to neighbouring unit or neighbouring detachment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "neighbouring detachment" does not appear there. What I'm trying to explain through my evidence is that this was the neighbouring detachment, six of whose wounded members we evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If we can return, please, to Exhibit 430, and paragraph 4, this order does not make any reference or does not describe the makeup of the assault detachment after the 14th of November, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what this order is about. It's the order that came after the previous one, and we looked at the previous one yesterday, and the previous one describes the exact structure of the assault detachment. The one that I have in front of me now, the only thing that happens here is that the motorised battalion is taken outside the detachment, leaving the structure, the composition, exactly the same as in the previous order, minus the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And this smaller 1st Assault Detachment, did it still comprise of assault groups?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It still comprised the Petrova Gora Detachment, the Leva Supoderica Detachment, and some support forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You've not answered the question, Mr. Stijakovic. You were asked if the 1st Assault Detachment after the 14th of November contained assault groups.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no further knowledge about the structure or composition of the assault detachment, especially in light of the fact that the assault detachment was still under the command of Major Tesic. Now, did he set up any assault groups by using the detachment and how exactly did he use these units is really not something that I can talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And even though you shared the same headquarters as Major Tesic and were responsible for making entries in the war diary, this was never discussed with you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To what specifically do you mean when you say "this was not discussed"? The contents of the war log?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: The composition of the 1st Assault Detachment and how it was made up after the 14th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the way I remember it. A unit like that might have been trying to do something, but the paramount thing was to carry out the assignment and to reach the water-tower, as stated in the order, and this is not something that they succeeded in doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Could I stop you there --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you make Milovo Brdo where you had a whole --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You're not answering the question you were asked which was did Major Tesic not discuss with you at any time the makeup of the 1st Assault Detachment after the 14th of November?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not discuss with me the makeup. Quite the opposite, in fact. He used to complain a lot. He complained about the fact that he did not believe the assignment would be that easy to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If this assignment to take the water-tower was so difficult, why, then, did Major Tesic not use Captain Radic and his successful company? Why did he send the TO Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because from as early on as the 10th of November, which is when the 1st Motorised Battalion had completed its task, the prevailing mood, atmosphere, the spirit among the men, in terms of going anywhere else outside of their previous area of assignment was weak, and people were not willing to go anywhere else. Tesic might have been minded to enlist Radic's assistance or somebody else's perhaps. It's just that he never told me. All he ever did was complain about this assignment of reaching the water-tower. He said that would be a very difficult task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Does that then mean that within the Guards Motorised Brigade, this elite unit that we've heard about, the soldiers did not want to fight; if they didn't feel like fighting, they were allowed to rest and do nothing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, I am the creator of what you are suggesting. It was me who was with the company commanders, having reached an important location like Milovo Brdo, when I pleaded, when I asked everyone else, when I proposed that we not go any further, since we've taken -- since we had taken all that we could. We had the whole town at our feet, and we had all the bridges under our control. It was only a matter of days when soldiers would refuse to fight on. Please try to understand how the mind of an average soldier works. The fighting goes on until a town is taken. After that, everything else is easily wrapped up. At this point, there was no reason remaining to keep on sustaining casualties, having our soldiers killed only in order to eventually reach the downtown area then. If you allow, what that means is it's not about lack of preparedness. It's not about any lack of fighting spirit. It's not about a drop in our morale. Quite the opposite, in fact. Everybody had the feeling that this thing was now over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You said they had the feeling that everything was now over. Was it not the case that casualties were sustained after the 18th of November and that orders were issued for you to be on high vigilance for fear of further activity from the defenders of Vukovar, pockets of resistance?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a war zone, when there are predictions or the likelihood that the battle would end, every life is valuable. And what you should do at a time like that, and this is precisely what we did, you should heighten the security measures, you should heighten the alertness, the awareness of the soldiers and try to forestall any form of surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If we can move on, please, Mr. Stijakovic. You have told us that Mr. Tesic was directly responsible for the Vukovar TO, Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora. They were subordinated to him. That's correct? That's your position?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, Major Tesic was in no position to command and control the TO, the Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora at the ground level, was he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not the impression that I had. Until the 18th of November, he had been trying to perform this task all the time, and that would be to get as far as the water-tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Major Tesic wasn't fighting at the front line, was he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes he would be at the very front line itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But only sometimes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Captain Radic, however, was at ground level, he was a company commander, he was involved in the fighting on a direct basis from day to day, and he was the man responsible, as the immediate superior, of the TO, the Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora up until the 21st of November; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can you please look at Exhibit 422, please? This, Mr. Stijakovic, is an order for resubordination on the 21st of November, 1999 timed at 6.00 a.m. from Colonel Mrksic and expressly resubordinates divisions of the Vukovar TO and withdraws and dispatches the Leva Supoderica to the 80th and 12th Brigades respectively. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could enlarge it a little bit. I can see it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 1 -- rather, if we start with the heading: "Regulating the issue of resubordination and return to the home units," and in paragraph 1: "The Leva Supoderica are dispatched to the 12th PMBR," and in paragraph 4: "The Vukovar TO units are resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade." Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this order for the first time now. I don't remember it from the war. But this is also part of this course of events that already was in place on the 18th of November, because on the 18th of November after the liberation of the city, all the units went back to their home units, and this order merely talks about further resubordination of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If Your Honour would allow me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we can move on from there just now. If you allow me, Mr. Stijakovic, I apologise but I do want to go back to that and just finalise one point. You're saying that this order of the 21st was part of a course of events that was already in place on the 18th of November. What do you mean by "already in place on the 18th of November"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 18th of November, when the action ceased and they ceased the moment when the other side surrendered, I mean the paramilitaries, all the units were brought back to their original state, to their home units, where they had been before the regrouping and resubordination and joining of units started. And in this order, the superior command, as you can see, lays ground for the handover of the entire territory to other units because the units that were there were about to return to Belgrade. Because you can see all the units that were temporarily attached to the Guards Motorised Brigade are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If you could please look at Exhibit 401, Mr. Stijakovic, in the Guards Motorised Brigade diary, and the entries for the 18th of November, 1991. That's L 0100533, page 38 in the English translation, and B/C/S page 02935477 -- 5479. I beg your pardon, 5477. Now, can you please look at the entry for the 18th of November and tell us whether there was any resubordination on the 18th of November, whether there is any reference to an order, whether it be oral or written?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which entry are you referring to, 0700 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If you could please look at all of the entries for the 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether there was any indication that there would be this resubordination. Is that what you meant? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stijakovic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and based on my analysis of this entry, we can see that the commander of the operations group invited the subordinate brigades and already started issuing orders for their independent action. In terms of the territory and the tasks were being coordinated here, you can see that at this meeting this issue was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, for the 18th of November, of which there are three separate entries, on page -- there are eight, sorry, separate entries for the 18th of November, in none of those 8 entries for the 18th of November is there any reference to resubordination with regard to the TO Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that it is not contained in the entry the way I just described it in the war log of the Guards Motorised Brigade, I don't know why it isn't there. It is my testimony that on the 18th, when combat ceased, the very next day, all the units went back to their peacetime stations. Specifically I'm talking about the Leva Supoderica Detachment and the Petrova Gora Detachment, and the order of the 21st merely provides a documentary basis for this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You gave evidence earlier today, Mr. Stijakovic, that an oral order was not authoritative when you spoke about the oral order of the 12th and the written order of the 14th of November. You said the oral order did not have any authority. Are you now changing that position?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said that an oral order is just as authoritative as a written order but once there is the written order, it is physically there, there is a material side to it, it's tangible, and there is no need any more to discuss the oral order because an oral order that was followed by a written order has been confirmed by this written order, which means that the oral order of the 12th confirmed in writing by the written order of the 14th, becomes legally valid because now there is the tangible written form thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I can move on, Mr. Stijakovic, to a new topic. You gave evidence yesterday that you attended at the Vukovar Hospital on the 19th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 19th of November, I was in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And you -- when did you first speak to the Defence team for Mr. Radic about these matters?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please specify your question so that I know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a matter of principle, yesterday, or perhaps it was today, when I asked Mr. Stijakovic whether he was in hospital on the 19th, the -- my learned colleague first said that I did not mention that in the summary and I withdrew my question. So something that was not mentioned in the examination-in-chief should not be brought up in the cross-examination. I don't really mind, but this is a matter of principle and principles should be complied with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I've mentioned before, Mr. Borovic, that if it goes to matters of credibility, or the advancement of the other party's case, the other party in cross-examination is not confined to the subject matter of the evidence in chief. And that is, as I see it, what is happening here. But there may be more that I haven't yet seen. We will find out. Mr. Lunny, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: To recap, Mr. Stijakovic, you told us yesterday that on the 19th of November, 1991, you attended at Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On the 19th --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in hospital on the 19th, and there is something that I told Mr. Borovic. As for the second part of your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: That was the second part of my question, Mr. Stijakovic. When did you first meet with the Defence team for Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with Captain Radic's Defence team in the capacity of a witness about five or six days ago, here in The Hague, and that was the first time that we discussed my going to the hospital, because one of the recordings, TV broadcasts, showed my face as -- showed that I was standing there in front of the hospital, and Mr. Borovic asked me whether I was in hospital and I said yes. So that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: The first time you spoke to the Defence was five or six days ago, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, about this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: When were you first contacted by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't be specific about the date, but the Defence contacted me immediately after Mr. Radic's decision to be represented before this Tribunal by Mr. Borovic's law office, and through my colleagues, more specifically my colleague Mr. Zirojevic, I was asked to come to the office for some consultations, and perhaps for potential testimony. I don't know the exact date. I know it was in the -- in summer, and I know that the first meeting was rather formal, and I would like to stress once again this is something that I told him too. I said that I wanted to testify but that I don't care who calls me as a witness, since I have already stated several times that I was the deputy commander of the battalion, I expected --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Could I stop you there, Mr. Stijakovic, I think you answered the question that was asked about when you met with the Defence and when you first spoke about the Vukovar Hospital. And it's your position it was merely five or six days ago, that's the first time you mentioned it to them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the first time that we discussed the hospital was during my last stay in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: With regard to that visit to the hospital, you told us that Radic was there on Tesic's orders; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To secure the wider perimeter of the hospital, that was the order that Captain Radic received from Major Tesic on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Major Tesic, as you said earlier, gave a statement to the ICTY, to the Office of the Prosecutor, in 2003, and he expressly stated that he gave no such order to Captain Radic and that Captain Radic was at the hospital of his own accord. Isn't it the case that there was no such order for Radic to be at that hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radic went to the hospital on express orders, and the presence of -- his presence and the presence of his soldiers is something that you can verify through testimony. As for what Tesic told you or anyone else about this going to the hospital is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I can move now to the 20th of November, 1991. You mentioned that the regular briefing at your headquarters for the 1st Motorised Battalion, the daily briefing, was held on the 20th as before. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, battalion.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about the 20th, whether there was a briefing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was the regular briefing in the evening of the 20th, at the headquarters of the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: What time was this briefing held at, Mr. Stijakovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was at around 2000 hours. It was night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And Captain Radic, he was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic was present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: What time did the meeting end at, Mr. Stijakovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting had two stages. In the first stage that was chaired by Major Tesic was the part when we defined the tasks for the 21st. He then left to the superior command in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Could you please stop, Mr. Stijakovic? I didn't ask you what the content of the meeting was. I merely wanted to know when the meeting ended.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm merely saying that it took about an hour and a half to deal with all that, an hour, an hour and a half, as far as I can remember, because we lingered there for a while after the meeting ended. After the commander left, we stayed there at the headquarters, and I remember that Captain Vuckovic invited us all for dinner at his place. He invited me. I couldn't go because Major Tesic was absent. But Staff Sergeant Bojic went with him. So some of the commanding officers there went to have dinner because they were invited by this captain. So I can't really tell you exactly how long this meeting took but anywhere between an hour and an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: This dinner you've referred to, did you tell this to the Defence of Captain Radic when you met them five or six days ago?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me -- I was asked whether I attended this dinner and my response again is I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: That wasn't the question you were asked, Mr. Stijakovic. You're avoiding the question. You've now made reference to a dinner on the 20th of November. This is the first we've heard about it. Did you mention that, did you tell the Defence of Mr. Radic when you met them five or six days ago that there was a discussion about a dinner on the evening of the 20th of November? It's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did tell the Defence that this dinner was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stijakovic. We can now move forward again. Could you please look at an article in Narodna Armija. It's in the e-court system and it's the -- has a reference 01147733, 01147784. Now, the magazine we are looking at, Narodna Armija, this was the official military magazine of the JNA, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Narodna Armija was the journal of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can we please look at page 10 in the B/C/S. The ERN number is 7742, which is page 1 of the English translation. And, Mr. Stijakovic, could you please read for us the first two paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but we cannot find the document in e-court, at least under this reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one copy. It was supposed to be placed in e-court and I have to apologise for that. I have one copy but it's marked with highlighting. If Your Honour would allow a very short recess I will obtain an unmarked copy that could perhaps be used with the witness and on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's desirable. Is it inconvenient to move to some other topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I only have one more question after this matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will take our break now, resuming at 25 to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I'm obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker's microphone please be adjusted? The interpreters cannot hear her.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke to my colleague, Mr. Lunny, and I heard that his cross-examination will last only for another five minutes or so, and in the redirect Mr. Borovic is going to take about 15 minutes. In the meantime, the OTP tried to interview the witness, and I asked to be given some notes regarding this attempt to have an interview. My colleague, Mr. Weiner, said that he would be examining or rather cross-examining that witness and he tried to speak to him. So I would appreciate it if I could receive some information now, as to whether the witness said something and what it was that he said, whether he wanted to give an interview or not, so that I would know whether I could start with the examination-in-chief today of that witness once this witness has completed his testimony. So I kindly ask you for your instructions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We approached the witness today through the victim witness unit. We notified that we received this morning some proofing notes with items that we had never previously received. As a result, we would like to speak to the witness. We -- the VW unit approached the witness and told him that the Prosecution would like to speak to him, that there were matters that he had recently given to the Defence that had not been raised previously by this witness, and he has refused, he will not speak, even though he had previously indicated that he would speak to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that examination can proceed this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We are very much obliged for the Court's accommodation in rising early to allow the difficulty with the article to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, before we get to that article, I've had the chance over the break to have a -- another look at your proofing note, proofing note that was provided to the Prosecution two days ago. And I'm looking at 10 different topics within that proofing note. Within those 10 topics, there is no mention at all of any dinner on the evening of the 20th. Now, either you didn't tell the Defence about that dinner, when you spoke to them five or six days ago, or you did tell them and it was left out. Which of those two positions is correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said what I had to say about that dinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, I've asked you a question and you must answer that question. The proofing note provided by the Defence to the Prosecution makes no reference to any dinner on the 20th of November, 1991. Now either you told them and it's been left out, or you did not tell them at all. Which of those two positions is correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told them about that dinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Are you telling the truth about that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I repeat once again? As for the dinner --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I'm not asking to you repeat your answer. I'm asking you, Mr. Stijakovic, if you're telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, under oath, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And is that the same standard of proof that you've been using all throughout today with regard to the rest of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If we can now move on, Mr. Stijakovic. When you left Vukovar and returned to Belgrade on the 24th of November, you were still second in command of the guards 1st Motorised Battalion. You had responsibilities for discipline. Were any officers investigated -- sorry, any officers of the Guards Motorised Brigade, were any of those officers investigated or punished for taking part in the killings at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Lieutenant Radovic was under investigation because his rifle had not been empty, and the first day, when he returned to Belgrade, one of his soldiers got killed. As for Ovcara and the question whether there was any investigation against any one of the officers, I was not aware of any such proceedings. I am actually saying that I did not hear of any proceedings related to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Just before the break, Mr. Stijakovic, you had mentioned your contact with the Defence and the role of Zoran Zirojevic. Can you please provide some details as to how -- or, rather, as to what Zoran Zirojevic did to put you in touch with the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He contacted me by telephone and he asked me whether I could come to the office of Mr. Borovic, the lawyer. That is all the work he had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And when did you receive that phone call from Zoran Zirojevic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can you provide us with the month that you were contacted by Zoran Zirojevic? Month and the year?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it must have been the year when Captain Radic had already arrived in The Hague, in the period when he was physically present here. I cannot remember that particular year now either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If we can now move on to look at the document that was provided during the break, Your Honour. I understand that it's 65 ter number 942. And copies, Your Honour, have been made available in English and in B/C/S to parties in the room. I understand the witness also has one to hand. And if I can ask Mr. Zirojevic [sic] to look at the article from Narodna Armija, which is entitled "Vukovar in the hands of the liberators."

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my name is Stijakovic, and you were asking Zirojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. Stijakovic. My mistake. Mr. Stijakovic, the article -- the first two paragraphs of the article reads: "Assault detachment commander Major Borivoje Tesic and his deputy, Captain First Class Slavko Stijakovic, discovered the frequency on which the members of ZNG, National Guards Corps, and MUP, Ministry of Internal Affairs, communicated and they intercepted their conversations with ease. One can easily hear from the black box in Tesic's hand that the ZNG -- sorry, the ZNG and the MUP members are suffering heavy artillery blows in the buildings of the city hall, MUP and municipal court, that the city hospital in the proximity has been spared as well as the city museum buildings near the Danube River. Major Tesic occasionally attempts to establish connection with Mile Dedakovic, also known as Jastreb, or Hawk, the commander of Vukovar Defence, to call on him to tell his subordinates to lay down arms in order not to devastate the so-called old Baroque heart of Vukovar and prevent hand-to-hand combat with additional victims. 'Jastreb, Jastreb, come in,' Tesic repeats, and waits in anticipation. Silence ensues. There is static coming from the gadget. Jastreb finally responds and asks Tesic what he wants. When he is given the conditions of surrender and guarantees that all prisoners unless they have blooded their hands on innocent people would be treated fairly Jastreb was silent for a moment. It seemed he was thinking but then refused the offer and started swearing and insulting. He was immediately told that he would get what is coming to him. And the thunder of successive explosions spread along the semi-arch of the fire line in the town depths." With regard to the passage in the second paragraph, "when he is given the conditions of surrender and guarantees that all prisoners unless they have blooded their hands on innocent people would be treated fairly, Jastreb was silent for a moment," Mr. Stijakovic, what was going to happen to defenders of Vukovar if they had blooded on their hands of innocent people?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rule of international warfare, they should have been brought before a court of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: In the article there is no mention of court of law, there is no offer of trial, simply a threat that only those who had no blood on their hands would be treated fairly; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear this conversation. This is a conversation that Major Tesic conveyed to the journalist, but even if I had heard it, I certainly would have taken steps on my part to have prisoners treated according to rules of warfare, and that they be taken before a court of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Oh, I beg your pardon, Your Honour, I wish to tender that 65 ter document as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am opposed - by your leave - to having this document admitted into evidence because no one confirmed the authenticity of this document. The witness says that he did not attend this conversation, that he was not present there, so for these formal reasons, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are there any other submissions? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will mark this document for identification at the moment, and will consider its admission in conjunction with the other media news concerning Mr. Hadzic, which is presently being considered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be marked for identification with the reference number 792.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stijakovic, today my learned friend asked you about fear in Vukovar, and he said to you that one witness had stated that fear was so great that it was palpable and that that was the reason why soldiers should not go to the front line. I am drawing your attention to page 12601, the witness said that this happened on the 2nd of October and that the fear in his first action was so great that it was palpable. He never said that it was a reason for --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I have an objection to my friend's question at this stage. He seems to be quoting the witness. I beg your pardon, Your Honour, I withdraw the objection. I see that the witness's name is not referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That witness -- I mean, if I tell you that that witness stated that it suited him fine to have members of the TO Leva Supoderica be on the front line and that his young men would be in the second line and that in this way he wanted to preserve their young lives, that is the real context that my learned friend did not want to put to you, but since he didn't put it to you I'm putting it to you. During this first march that your unit had, when they came to Vukovar, was there fear among these young men?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to the Prosecutor as well that that is a natural fear, a normal fear, that I felt too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And did it suit you as deputy commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion that later along the axis of this combat activity, young inexperienced soldiers should stay in the back, whereas the territorials would be in front either as guides or in cooperation or in any other way, not to go into that question now, that they go ahead?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part -- or, rather, most of the soldiers who secured the line that had been attained were precisely young soldiers. A certain number of them, the most courageous ones, were involved even in the front line of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the evening of the 20th, when Major Tesic left the briefing, you say that on the following day he was in Belgrade. So in that period, while Major Tesic was not there and while he did not take over his duty, was there any firing action or any kind of combat action on the part of the 1st Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, there was no such action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend of the Prosecution put it to you that before the Belgrade court some officers were convicted, the so-called Belgrade Ovcara. My question is: Have you heard of any officer in the Belgrade court being convicted because of Belgrade Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear of any officer convicted on account of Ovcara in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now just asking you about the 3rd Company that Miroslav Radic commanded. Although you spoke in detail, I would ask to you give me an unequivocal answer. The company of Miroslav Radic from that action on the 10th and 11th, when it was Milovo Brdo, until the 19th of November, was it a participant in any action in any other area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Radic's company remained at Milovo Brdo and that is where it ended its activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you say Milovo Brdo, are you referring to the area of Milovo Brdo and the neighbourhood of Bosko Buha, is it the same area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milovo Brdo is a geographical concept and around it and in that area is the neighbourhood of Bosko Buha as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend, my young friend, showed you today some notes that are part of the diary of the 1st Motorised Battalion. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a note and copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that this is not a verbatim copy but that you dictated to your soldier from this diary what you thought that you would need from your -- for your scholarly work?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that and I will tell you once again. From the content of the diary, I dictated the text and soldier Dobras did the writing. So this dictated text was corrected up to a certain degree in terms of the actual content of the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: My learned friend objected to you stating why, in these notes of yours, that are a copy of the diary but not a comprehensive copy, why you did not record the order of the 12th of November, 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is the following: In this copied notes, are there orders from the 16th and the 14th that we showed you here?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this copied version there is not a single written order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have already asked you whether you gave an interview to the OTP here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How long did it last approximately?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO  STIJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
